text: Current research has studied numerous variables regarding virtual assistants and how they are perceived.It was discovered by Osmers et al. [11] that human representations seem to have a positive impact on thesocial presence of a virtual assistant. Guo et al. [5] studied the effects of assistants having a similar voiceand appearance to the participant, concluding a higher co-presence and perceived intelligence but also moreeeriness with a self similar appearance. Studying the effect of appearance on robots, Strathearn and Ma [13]concluded that younger participants preferred younger looking robots for interaction and more senior onesolder looking versions. According to the results of Nam et al. [10], perceived usefulness and satisfaction andacceptance of virtual assistants is enhanced with providing expression. It was explicitly stated that genderimplications were not part of the experiment.Of course, gender was part of past research in the domain of virtual assistants: Kim et al. [7] studiedthe effects of gender and relationship type on conversational Agents and concluded no significant effectsof gender regarding competence, warmth or pleasure. It was stated, that this is contrary to past research.The experiment also studied casual conversation with voice agents, not embodiment or solving of tasks.The effects on gender when helping in a quiz assignment was studied with text-chat-based agents by Pfeuf-fer et al. [12]. It was concluded, that female representations were perceived more competent than malerepresentations in male knowledge fields, with the hint that this result could vary when interfacing over alonger period of time. That gender is an important trait was concluded in a literature review conducted byCraiut and Iancu [2]. Variables affecting perception and competence of gendered technology were identifiedin the research, with the comment that future research can explore these variables in an experimental approach.
